utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And for the appearances, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, and, Your Honour, Judge Hall. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Matthew Gillett, Case Manager Thomas Laugel, legal intern Ivana Parac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could the record reflect that we sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis, Judge Mindua being absent. The witness may be brought in. We go into closed session, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it the plan is now to go back to the cross-examination of Milinkovic -- Borivoje Milinkovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We're ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The witness may be brought in. Mr. Gillett, how long will you take? More or less, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Of course, it may depend on the length of the witness's answers. I'd estimate somewhere in excess of an hour but hopefully less than an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You may be seated, Mr. Milinkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Milinkovic, first of all, we want to apologise for the delay. The weather was good, so I hope it was not too bad for you. We'll continue with your cross-examination, and I have to remind you that you are still under oath. Mr. Gillett, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Before I get back into the substance of the cross-examination, I noted from your decision concerning this witness that the associated exhibits were accepted as relevant and probative and the basis was established for admission. But three of them do not appear yet to have been admitted when his 92 ter statement was admitted. These are 65 ter documents 1D1367, 1D1590, and 1D1296. And so I'd just like to verify if those will indeed be admitted as part of his 92 ter package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: As soon as you tender them which I suppose you do now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I had understood that the Defence were tendering them as part of the package but I'm certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Of course, I'm sorry. It's not -- it's not your documents. It's the Defence's documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The Defence only tendered two documents. But you are aware of that, and you are wondering whether the three other ones will be tendered as well. I don't -- I don't see any move from the Defence to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And this is the cause of my confusion. The usual procedure had been that where the associated exhibits listed in the Rule 92 ter filing were accepted by Your Honours as associated exhibits, they would be, can I say, automatically admitted, and I had understood that would be the procedure here. It is in the Defence hands if they want to include those as part of the 92 ter package. So if I could get clarification on that, the reason being otherwise I may seek to tender one or two of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I don't see any reaction from the Defence, Mr. -- oh, now there is. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we did not tender these documents, indeed, but as for one document's relevant for one other witness we would tender it with him. But -- and two other documents are indeed relevant for this witness, and as far as I recall, both of them were confronted -- no, maybe one of them was not confronted with -- the witness was not confronted with them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- but generally we could tender these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: In the 92 ter proceedings, Mr. Zivanovic, there's no particular need to show the documents to the witness again as they are considered to be linked with the statement. In that way, that statement becomes illegible or difficulty legible without the documents. So -- but it's up to you. You want to tender the three documents, two documents? One? None of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender two documents, two documents with this witness. It is his resignation and the one, the decision of the government --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you give the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I could say their numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, sorry. 1D1590 and 1D1296.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Those two documents are admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D195.187 and D196.187, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Milinkovic. Firstly, as minister of culture and religion in the government of the SBWS, your focus was on cultural and religious matters; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You didn't interfere with the work of other ministries; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: So the status of courts in SBWS, judicial courts, would be outside the work of your ministry; right?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: The SBWS did have civilian courts up and running in November 1991 that could try people for crimes against civilians; right?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were in the process of being established, but they could already work and hold trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I get document 1D1367, please. And this is tab 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a letter from Vojin Susa. He was the minister of justice in the SBWS government; right?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You discussed this letter in your statement and you provided it to the OTP when you were interviewed in 2003; right?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And for Your Honours' note, this is the remaining associated exhibit that the Defence did not tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: In the third paragraph, Mr. Susa states, and this is halfway in the -- down the paragraph: "It is certain that in all subsequent legal proceedings all persons who have committed crimes against the armed forces will be under the jurisdiction of military courts, but it is equally certain that persons who have committed crimes against the civilian population will have to be tried by the civilian courts that have subject matter and territorial jurisdiction, namely, the ones that already exist and function in the Serbian District." That matches with the evidence you just gave, doesn't it, that there were courts at that time in the SBWS?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. It is not the same. The Prosecutor mentioned the jurisdiction of the courts and it was about the existence of the courts. It is not the same. In my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness is capable of answering the question just as he answered my previous question as to whether there were courts up and running.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But it not reflect the content of the documents in previous answer -- previous question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: The -- I'll ask one more question before I get to the question I was going to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: The document says in the passage I just quoted: "... the ones," meaning the courts, "that already exist and function in the Serbian district," that matches the evidence you just gave a moment ago that there were courts that could already work and hold trials; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would tender 1D1367.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3262, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, on Thursday during your testimony, we discussed the meeting of 20 November 1991 in Velepromet; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You drove your own vehicle to the meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Was anyone with you in the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was somebody from my ministry, I believe an advisor, Djordje Ocic. The name just came back to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And you did not remember the name of the person with you when you gave your statement in 2003. That's right?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because during those days -- during these days while I was in the room, I cast my mind back to those details so it came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And you drove from Dalj through Borovo to Vukovar for the meeting but you were delayed for, I believe you said, 10 to 15 minutes because you stopped to look at damage to churches; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I made a turn to the Orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: At the Velepromet meeting, the main issue was the prisoners who had been arrested in Vukovar; right?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we play video P1731. This is tab 18, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "This is the first session of the government held in our future capital, the capital of our region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Regarding the conclusions, apart from the ones related to the normalisation of life and the establishment of a more or less normal situation, there is one basic conclusion that the prisoners, Ustashas with blood on their hands, cannot leave the territory of the Serb region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and they cannot be driven to Serbia, since Serbia is not at war. Also, the troops that assisted in the capturing, they are connected with the rest of the ... unclear ... those were not the soldiers who were captured, those were paramilitary formations, they can only be put to trial by these people here, that is the people of our Serb region, which is recognised, which has its courts. We even have a second-instance court, the third instance might possibly be on the federal level, the Yugoslav level, but we have our regional court and our municipal court. Consequently, we have agreed with the military authorities that those Ustashas remain in some of our camps here in the vicinity of Vukovar. Since one group was already taken to Sremska Mitrovica, I undertook the task to return those people here, if they can be called people at all, to return them, to bring them back, and to have them put on trial, to find out which ones among them are guilty, and those who are not shall normally be released so they can join us in the reconstruction of our town. "Reporter: How do you estimate the total number of those members of the Croatian paramilitary formations? There were different figures circulating. 200 surrendered two nights ago. Approximately 1.000 today in the Borovo complex. What numbers are we talking about? "Goran Hadzic: I believe the number is close to 3.000. Approximately 3.000 of mainly uniformed Ustashas, although there are still many hiding among the civilians. However, there are many honest people among them as well. Our primary task is to investigate everything and not to let anyone who is not guilty get hurt or be harassed. It is better to have one culprit slip through than to harm somebody innocent. That is our task. We have law enforcement and police forces and all the bodies here, so we will work to prevent any persecution of innocent people."

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: We will watch the remaining bit of the clip in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: But before doing so, Hadzic said that there was one basic conclusion from the meeting: "... that the prisoners, Ustashas with blood on their hands, must not leave the territory of the Serb region of SBWS and they cannot be driven to Serbia, since Serbia is a state which is not at war." And that's correct, that was the conclusion of the Velepromet meeting; right?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Was Hadzic not telling the truth when he made that claim?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It sounds like a political statement of his. First of all, I'm sure that that was not a session of the government, and if there had been such a conclusion, I would have had it in writing. I mean, from that session. But it was not connected to any sessions. This is just a political statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: My question wasn't whether it was a political statement. It was whether it was the truth, that there was one basic conclusion.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: So to clarify, Goran Hadzic was not telling the truth, in your evidence, in this interview?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did you -- did you watch Goran Hadzic's testimony a few weeks ago?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just noticed that the translation of this document did not reflect the whole -- the whole statement of Mr. Hadzic. Translation in e-court that was allegedly now presented to the witness has only two pages. And the particular pages where Mr. Hadzic spoke about the prisoners were not in e-court at all. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. President, my questions were based on the audio that had just been played that the witness listened to. I'm not aware of a problem with the translation or original of the transcript of this in e-court. If there is, we can certainly look at the break, and, of course, the Defence are welcome to raise this in re-direct, should they want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. In the transcript, there is a [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- are you speaking about the transcript of this video-clip or the transcript of the hearing today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I speak about both. Because the Prosecution referred to the P1731, and the P1731 as I read in e-court has not at all the parts showed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So that's the transcript of the video-clip. Okay. So that has to be clarified. Could --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We just like to see whether the P1734 was shown to the witness or something else. Because 1731, there is not the portion that were translated in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm looking at the transcript we have from e-court of P1731, and on the relevant point which I was asking the witness about, it says: "There is one basic conclusion, that the prisoners, Ustashas with blood on their hands," et cetera. It certainly appears to be the same to me as what was just read out. And we've watched this video in court a number of times. I'm -- this the first time I'm becoming aware that there may be some discrepancy. So, again, it's something that if the Defence wants to raise during the break, we're happy to look into it, but I don't see it as a reason to interrupt the questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll see that and whether we can resolve it during the break and get back to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Oh. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: My question, sir, was whether you had watched the testimony of Goran Hadzic a few weeks ago in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't follow the trial at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, although you say that Goran Hadzic's statement was not true, that there was a decision made to keep the prisoners in SBWS, the prisoners did, in fact, remain in SBWS, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could not command the military. The military decided as they did. So yes, you are correct in saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And they were killed at Ovcara, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that only much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: When did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few years later. I didn't know that they were all killed. And I learned that many years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You said a "few years later," and then "many years later." Can you be more specific and say when it was that you learned that the prisoners at Ovcara had been killed?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four or five years later, or perhaps three -- three years. Three years for sure. Maybe even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: At paragraph 54 of your statement, you say: "I first heard about the events that occurred at Ovcara around 1993. The first thing I heard was that some people had been killed there." That would be two years, at the most, later than the events in question, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, between 1990 and 1993 is a space of three years; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: No one was tried or prosecuted or investigated by the SBWS authorities for the mass killing at Ovcara, were they?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I don't know whether anybody -- anybody was ever put on trial for that. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we play the rest of P1731, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Today we have made a first step, we prepared ourselves for this step. I was a bit of an optimist, thinking that Vukovar was not so devastated. Today, when I saw it, I think there are no words to describe it but literally there is not a single undamaged house. There are even corpses out in the streets. Thus, we firstly have to have our Ministry of Health, actually, the agriculture, meaning the veterinary, the veterinarians and doctors have to prevent the contagion, to remove those, and then to start with the normalisation of life, which is already prepared. We had an agreement with those people today, the people who carried out the fights on their backs, those are the people from the settlement Petrova Gora, without whom, so to say, this fight of ours for Vukovar would have been lost. I am using this opportunity to thank them for everything they have done. We have scheduled the next meeting for tomorrow, with one group of ministers and the representatives of those people, to find bodies and to establish the civil rule in the town in an agreement with them. We have actually agreed with the representatives of the military authorities that the military rule shall not be established in Vukovar for a longer period, eventually only for a couple of days. But it is planned that the civil authorities take over the rule. "The interviewer: Does it imply that you will remove your uniform soon? "Goran Hadzic: Well, I am a person, the representative of the Serb people, who was elected by the Serbs. If the Serb people who appointed me believe that borders we have now established are satisfactory, I will remove it. But I personally believe that I should keep it on for some time, since the Serb borders are much further from where we stand now. "Thank you for this conversation."

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Goran Hadzic's description of the devastated state of Vukovar matches your own impressions when you first entered on 20 November 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: When Hadzic says: "Well, I am a person, the representative of the Serb people, who was elected by the Serbs," he doesn't refer to himself as a representative of the Croats in SBWS, does he?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what was on his mind at that moment. However, by just listening to his words, that seems to be the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And when he says: "If the Serb people who appointed me believe that the borders we have now are satisfactory, I will remove it. But I personally believe that I should keep it on for some time, since the Serbian borders are much further on from where we stand now," he doesn't refer to the interests of the Croat people in SBWS regarding the borders, does he?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never discussed borders so I don't know. We were still in Yugoslavia at that time. I don't know what he meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I see the time is for the break. Just one last question, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Since you were both members of the SBWS government, you and Mr. Hadzic both have a common interest in denying that your government had any discriminatory policies against non-Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. Let me explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Half of my family are Croats, as simple as that. The other half are Serbs. I never thought that they -- that Croats should be discriminated against because I would have to discriminate against my own mother and half of my family, and we all shared the same living space.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: To avoid any confusion, do I understand your evidence to be that you and Mr. Hadzic did not and do not have a common interest in denying that your government had any discriminatory policies against non-Serbs? Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you did not understand me. The only thing I shared with you was my own personal view. I don't know what Mr. Hadzic's position was or the position of the government for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. -- [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: sorry. I would object to the question because it implied that the government had a discriminatory policy and the witness never confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness has now answered, and I'm satisfied with the answer on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milinkovic, we'll take the second break. We'll come back in 30 minutes. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Just while the witness is being brought in, I discussed with my learned friend, and there is no problem with the transcript of the video, P1731. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, on Thursday in your testimony, you mentioned a Mr. Milorad Stricevic, and you said: "I know for a fact he was not a member of the military because he did some other things. I know -- I knew him from before the war." Stricevic was involved in criminal activities before the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And he spent time in prison; right?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You predicted my next question. We have a report here - that is P113.1, we don't need to show it right now - but it notes that Stricevic mistreated prisoners in Dalj in 1991. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did you know a Mr. Boro Berkovic?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Berkovic, not Boljkovic. Perhaps Borkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: He also --

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps Orlovic. I apologise. Orlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Again you have predicted my question. He also went by the name of Boro or Bora Orlovic. Was this gentleman from Dalj?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] And he spent time in Germany; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Apologies, I heard some interpretation coming through.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, you spoke to Bora Orlovic in October 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that I talked to him. I didn't really socialise with him. He was prone to committing crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we now get P113.1. And this is tab 37B. It's the public version of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And, sir, this is a report of the Vojvodina State Security from 15 October 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it is not -- it is not informed but -- report but information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I apologise. An information. We can call it an information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: On page 2.4, which should be page 3 in the B/C/S, it states the following: "Bora Berkovic, also known as Bosko Orlovic, a criminal from Borovo Naselje, had lived for many years in the SRN, Federal Republic of Germany, where he was involved in armed robberies and worked as a body-guard for Centar [phoen], a criminal from Belgrade. In a conversation, Berkovic claimed that Boro Milinkovic, minister for religions of the Slavonia, Baranja, and West Srem SAO, had offered him a certain amount of money in German marks to kill our source." Now, sir, you were the minister of culture and religion in October 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And you discussed killing this source with Bora Orlovic at that time, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, you were living in Dalj in 1993 still; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived in Dalj all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'm now going to turn to Exhibit P84.50. This is tab 6. It's an article from July 1993 describing an interview with Goran Hadzic. I have a blown-up version that I can provide to the witness if that is agreeable to my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, sir, I've -- the first passage that I've highlighted on page 1 about midway down --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And could we have this on the screen, P84.50, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: While it comes up, the passage that I'm interested in says: "During lunch, his body-guards sat at a neighbouring table and the guests were joined by Bora, nicknamed Vrlja (Cross-Eyes), who is a well-known fighter in this region, a member of the first government and minister for culture." That is you being described, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we turn to page 3 of the English which should be the next highlighted passage for yourself, the last column, second question down in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could you please zoom in on the text in B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Hadzic is asked: "How many Serbs are still in Croatia and do you still maintain links with them?" He answers: "Around 500.000 people live in the Republic of Serbian Krajina today. Thanks to Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, we have enough food and oil resources for everyone. Therefore we have all the conditions for normal life. As for the Serbs who have remained in Croatia, these are Serbs or, rather, the former leadership of the Communist party of which there are very few. The other Serbs who live in Croatia are Serbian fascists who support Tudjman. They are loyal to his authority and it is best that they remain there. An example of the former is Dusan Dragosavac, and the latter, Milan Djukic. There are a total of 50.000 such Serbs in Croatia. We do not need to co-operate with such so-called Serbs. As for the Croats in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, I do not know their number but few stayed here." "Q. You have broken with some close associates. Why? "A. The difference was obvious. For example, with some Serbs from Western Slavonia. An example is Veljko Dzakula who sometimes secretly negotiates with the Croats. He was in the government but our concepts of the struggle were different from the beginning. He and his supporters are no longer any kind of political force. They wanted to go with cohabitation with the Croats, and we wanted to be neighbours only. When it comes to Zdravko Zecevic, a former government member, he is an honest Serb, but at one point he cannot find a solution. For us, cohabitation with the Croats is treachery. We will never agree do this, even if a new war begins." Firstly, by this date, July 1993, is it correct that there were very few Croats who were remaining in the RSK, Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can talk about my region. Very few of us were left. I can't give you a broader picture. I can only talk about where I lived. I did not have information as to what was going on in other parts of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And to clarify, when you say "very few of us," do you mean very few Croats?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, I'm talking about only about the area where I lived. I can't say anything about any of the other parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: When Hadzic refers to the Serbs remaining in Croatia - meaning Croatian-controlled Croatia - he labelled these people as traitors effectively based on where they were located; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment on what Mr. Hadzic might have thought and whether this is authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: So you cannot comment on what he meant when he talked about cohabitation; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I don't even remember that he said this. All I know is what I'm reading from a newspaper. I cannot talk about things I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you joined Hadzic during this interview or not?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that day, it was in Bogaljevci. I joined them. There was Mr. Gulan whom I had been friends with for many years even before the war. That's the man who wrote this interview. But it was informal. It was talk over lunch, and I can't remember all the things that were said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And this article describes you as a well-known fighter in the region, not a pacifist; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, journalists, to make themselves important for making the interview, liked to describe everybody as a fighter or a commander. Gulan knows very well what kind of man I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: When you were testifying on Thursday last week, you were asked: "Q. Do you recall a referendum as to whether the Serbs want to remain within Yugoslavia or be annexed to some other country? "A. No, no, no. We always wanted to remain within Yugoslavia." That's at transcript page 11329. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You went to Borovo Selo several times in July 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I have another article. It's P3226. Again, I've blown it up, so if my friends are agreeable, I'll pass this to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: This is an article from 16 July 1991, describing the situation in Borovo Selo and the SBWS. Now, if we look at the bottom of page 1 in English --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And could we get this on the monitor. This is P3226, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we look at the bottom of page 1 in English, which should be on the second page -- sorry, you only have one page in the blown-up version. But for the electronic version it's the second page of B/C/S. And it states: "Instead of having a national council, Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem have since recently had their own government. Goran Hadzic, its president, says that its first task is for these areas to be joint to Serbia as soon as possible." It doesn't mention remaining within Yugoslavia, does it?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not mentioned here explicitly but it's a reference to Yugoslavia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we move to the bottom of page 2 in the English version, and this is the second-last box of text in the B/C/S, it states: "Goran Hadzic announced an impending general Serbian uprising in that part of Croatia, so 'everyone would share the same fate.'" The Serb take-over of Dalj, in fact, occurred several days after this article was published; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this statement, I wasn't aware of this statement. I'm seeing it for the first time, and I knew nothing about any impending uprising. We never discussed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: My question was about the dates. The article referring to Hadzic's announcement is 16 July 1991, and the take-over of Dalj, which you have referred to earlier in your testimony, occurred several days after that, on 1st of August; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, that ends my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gillett. Re-direct, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milinkovic, in response to the questions from the Prosecution, you said, among other things, regarding that time when Goran Hadzic and Arkan arrived in Vukovar. I remember that series of questions. You saw them together, you said. Can you tell where you saw them together in Vukovar on 20th November?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, they were inside by the entrance, standing shoulder to shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean by the entrance. Was it outside?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I mean indoors, in the room where the meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see some video footage or maybe photographs from that meeting in Velepromet, in the yard of Velepromet, where Goran Hadzic and Arkan and some other people were filmed?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor has shown you one video-clip, number 46038.2 [as interpreted]. I'll repeat the number: 6338.2. And you are in that footage too, remember?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There were some objects on the table in front of you, some lighters, and some other small items. And on them was the acronym NDH. What's the meaning of that acronym?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means "Nezavisna Drzava Hrvatska," the Independent State of Croatia. Our associations with that acronym are the times of Ante Pavelic and all the atrocities that happened to us at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On one of those objects there was a letter U. What did that mean?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That meant "Ustasha." It was an army allied with Hitler.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell at that time, to the best of your knowledge, did there exist any groups in Croatia that openly called themselves Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I also noticed some inscription that said: "Bitter herbs on a bitter wound."

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And below that, "poglavnik," chieftain. What does this word, "poglavnik," mean for both Croats and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That meant Ante Pavelic, the Ustasha chief, the leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Those objects that were filmed and photographed, that happened to be in front of you there, where had they been found? How did they arrive there?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got that from the people who had been captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Last Thursday and earlier today you mentioned Milorad Stricevic. Can you tell us, did he live in Dalj from before the war? How long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've known him for a very long time. He lived for a long time in Osijek before coming to Dalj. He married in Dalj and continued to live there. I don't recall that he was politically active, except that when we were establishing the SDS, he was setting up the Movement for Yugoslavia. The full name is League of Communists - Movement for Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also received some questions regarding the protest held on the 15th of October, 1991, in Dalj. Did you hear any minister say that he had attended that protest?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. But I heard from some local residents in Dalj that they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, at that time, apart from you, was there any other minister living in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There were also some questions about the destruction of the Catholic church in Dalj, and you said that you were emotionally attached to the Catholic church in Dalj. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I grew up in my childhood in that neighbourhood close to that church. That's where we played. And on some saint's day, we had the custom of going to the Catholic church, just like the Catholic church -- Catholic people went to our church on some holidays, so I was emotionally attached to it because of my childhood memories.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier today that one of -- part of your family are Croat. Who would that be?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Half of my family. My mother, my uncles, my cousins, my aunts. We all lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also answered some questions regarding Mr. Calosevic, and it was put to you that he had mistreated non-Serbs. How did he treat Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a conflictual person, very -- very short-fused. It was difficult even for Serbs to deal with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what was his relationship with Goran Hadzic? How did he act with Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Djoko, how did he treat Mr. Hadzic? Condescendingly. Condescendingly. That was his style.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he perhaps pin a nickname on Mr. Hadzic? Maybe not openly addressed him with that nickname but used it on other occasions.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a cheeky nickname that he didn't use especially provocatively. We all understand that kind of humour. He called him Klato or Gogi.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing else?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing that I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if he ever served as Goran Hadzic's body-guard?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure he never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also spoke during cross-examination about something that happened in Dalj in the course of 1992, the expulsion of Croats from Dalj, and you said that after that happened, you learned more about it from a Croat man who had also been among those expelled and came to visit you. What exactly did he tell you and why did he come to visit you in the first place?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came to see me, just to see me. During one time in my life, I was rather well-known in the community and I was on good terms with both Croats and Serbs. So he just felt the need to see me and to tell me about those events, and he told me about those people who expelled the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you on that occasion that you and your brother had also taken part in this?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, he couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You made a statement to the OTP, and you were asked questions about that statement. Before signing that statement, did you have the opportunity to read it in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was read back to me. I didn't read it myself because I don't know English, so I signed what a person read back to me, but I didn't see anything in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Earlier today, we heard a question about the discriminatory policies. Did you hear that the government pursued such policies against the Serbs [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we never discussed things in that way. There were a lot of Croats who were in it together with us so there was no justification for talking like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to correct my own question: "Did the government pursue such policies against the Serbs?" I meant non-Serbs. I want to avoid any confusion. Can you please repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were a lot of Croats in the police. For example, Luka Cuncic [phoen] was a mechanic, a Croat, and my friend. He was a member of the civilian protection as well. So we did not pursue any such policies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Goran Hadzic advocating discrimination of non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Even in private conversations with Mr. Goran Hadzic, even when we joked around, he would take the mickey out of me on that account. But he never spoke negatively about Croats. He did speak negatively about Ustasha but not Croats as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were shown an interview taken by a journalist whose name was Gulan, I believe. Were you aware of that interview being recorded or was he making notes during the interview?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Branislav Gulan often came to my place. He wanted to take notes, and he loved taking notes. And on that day, there was lunch. I happened to be there. I saw him, and I approached that table. Not because of Mr. Goran Hadzic who was also there, but because of him, because we were good friends. The atmosphere was very relaxed, it was a friendly atmosphere, there was a lot of joking around. Nobody recorded anything. It was not a formal interview. Nobody took any notes, or at least I don't remember any such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: One more thing that I wanted to ask you. During the cross-examination you said that a lot of Croats -- or, rather, non-Serbs left the area where you lived. How many Serbs left at the same time; do you know?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite a lot of Serbs left as well. I wouldn't know how many. I wouldn't be able to give you a figure, but many left. Many went to Germany, others to Austria. Quite a few of them went to Serbia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That would be all. Thank you, Mr. Milinkovic.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I've finished my re-direct, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not sure if you had further questions. If not, the Prosecution would respectively ask to ask two very short questions just to clarify something that came out during the re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Go ahead. Very shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. Much obliged.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milinkovic, this brings your testimony to an end. We thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey home. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is the next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we don't have the witness. The next witness is not ready for today. He will come tomorrow. We didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: He will be there tomorrow morning at 9.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Bad eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: There's too many of us here. Your Honour, good afternoon. With respect to the next witness, we do have an issue to raise which just came up this morning. We received a two-page proofing note which you must have received as well. There are a number of problems that arise out of this proofing note. First of all, we note that the witness was proofed over the weekend, on the 13th and 14th of September, and we only received the proofing note this morning, two days after the end of the proofing. At least that's what the proofing note states here. So our first concern is that we receive proofing notes as soon as possible in order to prepare. Secondly, we noticed the length. Now, this witness is coming as hybrid, a 92 ter hybrid witness. His statement is four pages and this proofing note is two pages long, pretty much 50 per cent of the length of the proposed 92 ter statement. We submit, Your Honours, that it defeats the purpose of Rule 92 ter if in preparing these statements, counsel are not thorough in asking questions to their 92 ter witnesses. We have noticed that this witness was met twice this year. First in April and then in the month of May to review and sign his statement. There is no reason for statements which are purposely prepared for this case not to be thoroughly explored with the witnesses. Now, we object to the practice and especially in the circumstances where the proofing notes come at the last minute and we have to prepare, investigate, and look into the new material that is coming across. And, finally, Your Honours, there are two documents that are mentioned in this proofing note which we have not been provided yet. We requested them this morning and we have not received a copy. So as can you see, there are a number of layers of complications with this proofing note. And our point is that, first of all, we be given advance notice or be given the proofing notes as soon as possible, and that the documents be provided as well, and that, again, 92 ter statements be prepared as fully as possible to avoid such problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I could just answer that I missed the date 15 of September, when I also met the witness. It is not written in my proofing note. As to other issues, I went with -- through -- through this statement with the witness, and he gave me some additional information. I put it in the proofing notes, and that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And he didn't do so in April or in May, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Such information, I have no such information in April or in May. I got it here when proofing him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And what about the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: These documents are, as far as I know, in e-court. Maybe they are -- they have not been released yet. Both documents are very, very short, just in few lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, do I understand that your intervention is to avoid this kind of problems in the future?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes. It's, number one, to avoid such problems in the future to have 92 ter statements in a more thorough fashion. But the documents themselves, the proofing note does not indicate their 65 ter numbers. We sent an e-mail shortly after starting court at 9.00 this morning to request these two documents and we still have not received them five hours later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It will be released as soon as possible. I think immediately after the sitting. And I'm really not able to foresee what would the witness say during the proofing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. We are discussing the documents now, so what you are telling us is that the Prosecution will have them, let's say, within a half an hour after the hearing? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Demirdjian, would that be sufficient for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, for this time I believe that since cross-examination is not going to take place today, I hope that I will be able to cover all the issues in the proofing note. Perhaps our relief at this stage is to remind the Defence and warn them to avoid such situations again in the future. I would say that half of the proofing note alone is probably issues which expand on topics in the statement but there is also quite a lot of information which is new. And that's where we face a problematic situation. We have a prejudice in terms of investigating and looking around this information less than 24 hours before the witness takes the stand. So that is perhaps our relief at this stage to remind the Defence of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I may respond. I don't believe that there was new information in my proofing notes. These are just clarification of what the witness said. I don't know, I'm not aware of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We will not --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- any new information he gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We will not start a discussion on that for the moment, Mr. Zivanovic. But I think that I voiced the warning that Mr. Demirdjian asked for even if I didn't speak it out explicitly. But we understand each other, don't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Demirdjian -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer. Definitely bad eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, apologies, one last small housekeeping matter and this is, I think, at the suggestion of the Registry. Last week we had an MFI document that was then admitted into evidence as P3252, once the translation was -- was corrected and put into e-court. And I have been asked just to note for the record that the document ID number for that is 0184-6450-ET. And that relates to what is now Exhibit Number 3252, P3252, which had been 65 ter 1939.13. So I hope I've said all the numbers that I'm supposed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And these are -- this is the corrected translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The verified one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I believe there was a missing footnote that has now been restored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I remember, the missing footnote issue. So if there is no objection, we will lift the -- the marked for identification ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And we would replace it with the -- with a new exhibit number. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I would just inform the Court that we released two documents. Two documents requested by Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. If that is all -- the new exhibit number, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: There is no new exhibit number. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 17th day of September, 2014, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.50 p.m.,
